questions.prompt: An \(n\)th-order differential equation is written as a state model. How many states does that take?
questions.explanation: Each extra derivative needs its own initial condition, so an \(n\)th-order equation has \(n\) states. One equation can still hide several derivatives. A and B are matrices, not a count of states. The number of entries in A is \(n^2\), which counts coefficients, not states.

options: n, one per derivative you have to remember
1, because one equation is one state
n squared, the number of entries in A

questions.prompt: A mass \(m = 4\), damper \(b = 6\), and spring \(k = 10\) obey \(m\ddot{y} = u - b\dot{y} - ky\). With states \((y, \dot{y})\), the lower-left entry of \(A\) is
questions.explanation: Divide through by \(m\): \(\ddot{y} = -(k/m)y - (b/m)\dot{y} + u/m\). The coefficient of \(y\) in the \(\dot{x}_2\) row is \(-k/m = -10/4 = -2.5\). The damper term \(-b/m = -1.5\) is the other entry of that row. The positive ratio \(k/m\) drops the sign that the restoring force requires.

questions.prompt: Same mass-spring-damper, \(m = 4\). The input \(u\) is the force. The lower entry of \(B\), the coefficient of \(u\) in \(\ddot{y}\), is
questions.explanation: The force is divided by the mass, so that entry is \(1/m = 0.25\). The spring and damper do not multiply \(u\). Using \(m\) itself, or \(k/m\), puts a different coefficient in the input column.

questions.prompt: Same device, \(m = 4\), \(b = 6\). The lower-right entry of \(A\), the coefficient of \(\dot{y}\) in \(\ddot{y}\), is
questions.explanation: That entry is \(-b/m = -6/4 = -1.5\). The spring entry \(-k/m\) does not multiply \(\dot{y}\). Dropping the minus sign gives the damping ratio's ingredients with the wrong sign, and the free response would then grow.

questions.prompt: The output equation of a state model is
questions.explanation: \(y = Cx + Du\) reads the output off the state, plus any piece that jumps straight through from the input. \(\dot{x} = Ax + Bu\) is the state equation, not the output. Swapping \(x\) and \(y\) inverts the definition. Using A and B for the output mixes the two equations.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a C row and a D entry, symbolic</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">c1   c2</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">d   0</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A symbolic array, not a numeric answer.

questions.prompt: Same \(A\) and \(B\) as above (\(m=4\), \(k=10\), \(b=6\)). A constant force \(u = 8\) is applied. At rest, the position \(y\) is
questions.explanation: At rest \(\dot{y} = 0\) and \(\ddot{y} = 0\), so \(0 = -(k/m)y + u/m\). Then \(y = u/k = 8/10 = 0.8\). Dividing by the damper instead of the spring gives \(8/6\). Multiplying force by mass gives 32, which is not a position.

questions.prompt: A diagonal state matrix has entries \(-2\) and \(-8\) on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. The slower eigenvalue (the one closer to zero) is
questions.explanation: On a diagonal matrix the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries. The slower decay is the one closer to the origin, \(-2\). The \(-8\) mode dies four times faster. Their sum \(-10\) and their product \(16\) are coefficients of the characteristic polynomial, not the slower mode.

questions.prompt: You rewrite the same ODE in a new choice of states. Which statement stays true?
questions.explanation: A change of coordinates \(x = Tz\) replaces \(A\) by \(T^{-1}AT\). Similar matrices share their eigenvalues, so the modes do not move. A itself does change unless \(T\) commutes with it in a trivial way. B is transformed too, and it is not forced to be the identity.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a state matrix with the bottom row still open</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   1</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">?   ?</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with the second row not filled in.
options: A is unchanged, because the physics did not change
the eigenvalues change to the new coordinates

questions.prompt: For \(m=4\), \(b=6\), \(k=10\) and states \((y,\dot{y})\), the characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^2 - \mathrm{tr}(A)\,\lambda + \det(A)\). The coefficient of \(\lambda\) is
questions.explanation: That coefficient is \(-\mathrm{tr}(A)\). The diagonal of \(A\) is \(0\) and \(-b/m = -1.5\), so the trace is \(-1.5\) and the coefficient is \(1.5\). The constant term \(2.5\) is \(\det(A) = k/m\), not the coefficient of \(\lambda\). The bare trace \(-1.5\) still carries the sign of the diagonal.

questions.prompt: A one-state model for a later free-response calculation is \(\dot{x} = -x/3\). The eigenvalue is
questions.explanation: The equation is \(\dot{x} = ax\) with \(a = -1/3\), so the eigenvalue is \(-1/3\). The positive \(1/3\) would grow. The reciprocal \(-3\) swaps the time constant with the rate.

questions.prompt: A realization of a third-order transfer function, with no pole-zero cancellation, uses how many states?
questions.explanation: Each pole needs a state if nothing cancels. A third-order denominator has three poles, so the realization has 3 states. A second-order pattern would leave a pole out. The number of coefficients in a generic \(3 \times 3\) matrix is 9, which is not the state count.

questions.prompt: The modes of a linear state model are
questions.explanation: Each mode is \(e^{\lambda t}\) for an eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(A\), with a shape given by the matching eigenvector. The columns of B say how inputs reach the states. The rows of C say which combination is measured. Sensor time constants are extra poles you add only if you model the sensor.
